opus-5.5.text:
I think one of the useful ways to understand it is that the internet isn't just a pile of text. It's a record of people solving problems. When someone writes a forum post debugging their code, or explains a proof, or argues about history, they're leaving behind a trace of a fairly sophisticated cognitive process. When you train a model to predict that text really well, the cheapest way to do it eventually stops being memorizing surface statistics. It becomes modeling the process that generated the text. So a lot of what looks like emergence is the model being pushed, by sheer prediction pressure, into representing the latent structure behind the data: the reasoning, the intentions, the world knowledge that people were drawing on.

The "emergent" part, the sense that capabilities show up suddenly, I think is partly real and partly about how we measure things. If your metric is "did you get the whole multi-step answer exactly right," then gradual improvements in each step can look like a sharp jump at the end. But there's also something genuine there. Some capabilities really do require several component skills to come together, and until they all reach a certain level you just don't see the composite behavior.

The thing I'd emphasize, coming from robotics, is that this works because the data is a proxy for human experience. People have already done the hard work of interacting with the world, and what comes out the other end is distilled into language. The model gets to piggyback on that. That's both the strength and the limitation. The model inherits the structure of human problem-solving, but it's learning from the residue of experience, not the experience itself. It never had to act, see the consequences, and correct itself.

That's why I think the next frontier is figuring out how to get that same kind of emergence from data where the model is actually in the loop, where it's acting in the world, whether physically with robots or in some other environment, and learning from the outcomes. Internet data gives you an incredible prior. But I suspect the really robust, adaptive capabilities come when you combine that prior with learning from your own interaction.

r001.rationale: The response says composite capabilities can appear when several component skills reach a sufficient level, but it does not identify generalization becoming compositional as the source of emergence.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I think about this is that it's actually a little bit of a misnomer to call them emergent, at least in the sense that people sometimes mean it, which is that something comes out of nowhere. I think a better way to think about it is that the internet is produced by people, and people are intelligent agents trying to accomplish things in the world. So when you train a model on internet data, what you're really doing is you're distilling a kind of compressed representation of the processes that generated that data. And those processes are human cognition, human problem solving, human communication.

So if the model is doing a good job of predicting that data, in some sense it has to acquire some approximation of the underlying machinery that produced it. That's where a lot of the capabilities come from. It's not that the model spontaneously invents reasoning. It's that reasoning is latent in the data, because the data was produced by things that reason.

Now, I'd put a caveat on that, which is that there's a big difference between acquiring a representation of how people solve problems and actually being able to solve problems yourself in a new situation. The internet gives you the former. It gives you a kind of enormous library of patterns about how problems have been solved. What it doesn't give you nearly as much of is the experience of trying things, failing, and figuring out what actually works for you. And that's the part where I think people sometimes overestimate what pretraining alone buys you. The capabilities look emergent because the scale lets the model pull together things that were there in the data but scattered, and at a certain point it can connect them. But the ceiling is set by what humans already did and wrote down.

That's actually why I think the reinforcement learning side, or more generally learning from the model's own experience, matters so much. If you want capabilities that go beyond what's in the data, the model has to actually interact with something and get feedback. Otherwise you're always just interpolating within the space of things that people have already done.

r001.rationale: The response says that at sufficient scale the model can connect patterns that were scattered in the data, presenting that as why capabilities appear emergent. This conveys compositional capability emerging once the model reaches a threshold.

astra-6.text:
I think the starting point is that predicting text well is a much harder problem than it sounds. The training objective is simple to state, but the process that produced the text is not. People write things because they have beliefs, intentions, and some understanding of how the world works. If you want to predict what they write across a sufficiently broad range of situations, it helps to recover some of that underlying structure.

Imagine you're predicting the next line in a description of someone solving a math problem. You could memorize patterns of what solutions look like. But at some point, actually doing the calculation becomes a better way to predict the answer. The capability isn't explicitly specified in the objective, but it becomes useful for satisfying the objective.

That gives us a plausible explanation for why capabilities develop. It doesn't necessarily explain why they sometimes appear suddenly. Some of that could be the way we measure them: a model might improve gradually, but if a task requires several steps to all be correct, you don't see much success until each step is sufficiently reliable. Some of it could also reflect a change in the strategy the model learns. I don't think we have a complete account of that.

The interesting question to me is how far this goes. How much understanding of the world can you acquire from observing what people say about it, and where do you need to act and see the consequences? Internet text provides an enormous amount of indirect experience. But it's still a particular view of the world, selected and described by other people.

r001.rationale: The response says broad text prediction can reward learning underlying structure and doing calculations, but it does not identify generalization becoming compositional at a sufficient level as the source of emergent capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think part of the mystery comes from treating prediction as a very simple task. Predicting the next word sounds simple, but the process that generated that word might be quite complicated. It might involve a person reasoning through a problem, writing a program, or describing something they’ve observed in the world. To predict that well, a model benefits from recovering some of the underlying structure of that process.

Imagine you’re predicting the next move in a chess game. You could learn statistical regularities about which moves tend to follow which other moves. But at some point, being able to evaluate the board and anticipate what the players are trying to do becomes a better way to predict. The training objective hasn’t changed, but the strategy for satisfying it has become much more sophisticated.

I suspect something similar happens with internet data. There are many tasks implicitly represented in that data, even though we haven’t labeled them as tasks. As the model becomes more capable, learning reusable mechanisms for solving those tasks can become more effective than learning lots of isolated correlations.

Now, that doesn’t necessarily explain why a particular capability appears at a particular scale. And we should distinguish a capability that really develops abruptly from one that improves gradually but only becomes visible once it crosses some threshold on our evaluation. But I don’t think we need a separate source of supervision to explain why prediction can produce surprisingly general capabilities. The structure of the processes you’re trying to predict can provide a great deal of supervision on its own.

r001.rationale: The response says models may learn reusable mechanisms instead of isolated correlations, but it does not clearly identify generalization becoming compositional at a sufficient level as the source of emergent capabilities.
